wine.name: Octagon
wine.grapes: Merlot, the larger part in most vintages read, with Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot and at times Cabernet Sauvignon, which led the 2007; the shares change each year.
wine.sites: The estate's own vineyards around the ruins of Governor James Barbour's house at Barboursville, in the rolling hills of Orange County, within the Monticello AVA.
wine.making: Each grape is fermented apart on its skins in stainless steel for six to ten days, with a longer maceration after. The wine is aged for about a year in French oak barriques, part of them new; the chosen barrels are then blended and rested in steel for about six months before bottling. It is made only in vintages the house holds equal to it.
wine.glass: Blackcurrant, raspberry and blueberry over cedar, sweet tobacco and a little toasty oak; medium to full in body, with fresh acidity, fine, silky tannin and a dry, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Open within a few years of release, a strong vintage gains savoury depth over a decade and more.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle an hour ahead; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: Named for the eight sided drawing room at the heart of Jefferson's design for Governor Barbour's house.
The state of origin, as most vintages print it; some have carried the Monticello AVA, in which the estate lies.

records.table: Thomas Jefferson drew an eight sided room for Governor James Barbour's house, whose ruins stand on the estate, and Barboursville Vineyards named Octagon for it: a Bordeaux style red from Orange County, mostly Merlot, made only in the years the house thinks worthy.
records.story: James Barbour (1775 to 1842), governor of Virginia through the War of 1812 and later Secretary of War, built his house at Barboursville to designs supplied by his friend Thomas Jefferson (1743 to 1826); it stood complete by about 1822, with an octagonal drawing room at its heart. On Christmas Day 1884 it burned, leaving the brick walls and the columns of its porticoes, which stand as a listed landmark. In 1976 the Zonin wine family of the Veneto, whose firm dates its roots to 1821, bought the estate as its one wine estate outside Italy. As the house tells it, officials and bankers alike advised it to plant tobacco; it set European vines instead, where Jefferson's own at Monticello had failed. Octagon was first made with the 1991 vintage, from older plantings, and again in 1995, before the 1998, a strong Virginia year, was made in quantity enough to sell widely. It is left unmade in years the house judges weak, so a run of Octagon has gaps. Octagon carries the story of Virginia wine from Jefferson onward, and it is the bottle to name when a guest asks what Virginia does with the Bordeaux grapes.

others.name: Viognier Reserve
others.note: A white of the Rhône grape that Virginia named its signature in 2011.

others.name: Nebbiolo Reserve
others.note: A red of Piedmont's grape, one of the Italian varieties the Veneto founders brought to the estate.

others.name: Petit Verdot Reserve
others.note: A varietal red of a grape that also goes into Octagon, made in the house's reserve range.

traps: Octagon is a blend of the Bordeaux grapes, not a varietal, and Barboursville's Italian grapes go into its other wines.
The house at Barboursville was designed by Jefferson for James Barbour; it is not Monticello, Jefferson's own home near Charlottesville.
Octagon is not made every year: the house leaves it unmade in vintages it judges weak.

wine.name: Viognier
wine.grapes: Viognier, the white grape of Condrieu in the northern Rhône.
wine.sites: The house's vineyards around Gordonsville in the rolling hills of Orange County, where Viognier was chosen for its thick skins and loose clusters, which resist the rot of humid Virginia summers.
wine.making: Made from Viognier grown by the house in Orange County. Its Barrel Select bottling is given time in oak, which by the house's account lifts the palate and leaves a finish of green apple. The first wines were made in a leased cellar before the house crushed in its own in 1993.
wine.glass: Ripe apricot, peach and honeysuckle with gardenia and a hint of ginger; round and generous in texture, with modest acidity and a soft, scented finish.
wine.ageing: Made to drink young, in its first two or three years, while its perfume is fresh.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass with room for the perfume.

label.means: The grape, which Virginia named its signature grape in 2011.
The house's bottling of the grape given time in oak before release.

records.table: Horton Vineyards of Gordonsville in Orange County helped make Viognier Virginia's white: its founder chose the Rhône grape for thick skins against the humid summers, and its 1992, by the house's medal list, won its class in San Diego. Drink it young, a little cool.
records.story: By its own account the house began in 1989, when its founder and a business partner bought land at Gordonsville in Orange County, after a small home vineyard in Madison County from 1983. Having studied Viognier in the Rhône and in California, he bet on it for its thick skins and loose bunches, which shrug off the rot that summer rain brings to Virginia, and he was among the first in the state to plant it. He planted Norton too, bringing the native grape of Richmond back to Virginia from Missouri in 1989, as Virginia Wine tells it. The first small crop came in 1991 and was made in a leased cellar, Montdomaine; the first crush in the house's own cellar followed in 1993. By the house's medal list its 1992 Viognier won its class at the San Diego National Wine Competition of 1994, a prize that turned other growers towards the grape, and in 2011 Virginia named Viognier its signature grape. The founder died in 2018. In 2019 the house's Petit Manseng of 2016 won the Governor's Cup, the first time that grape took the overall prize. Virginia's Viognier starts here, at a house that has always grown the unusual.

others.name: Norton

traps: Horton replanted Norton commercially; the grape itself was raised in Richmond in the 1820s, long before the house.
Horton is at Gordonsville in Orange County, the same county as Barboursville, not in the northern hunt country around Middleburg.
The Governor's Cup of 2019 went to Horton's Petit Manseng, not to its Viognier.

wine.name: Hardscrabble Chardonnay
wine.grapes: Chardonnay alone, drawn from the Hardscrabble vineyard with vines planted in 1985 and later; some vintages blend in fruit from the house's other sites.
wine.sites: Hardscrabble, the estate vineyard around the winery on top of the Blue Ridge at about 1,350 feet, on south and east facing slopes of mixed shale, granite and greenstone; by the house's account the greenstone's silt and clay suit its white grapes.
wine.making: Fermented and aged in French oak barrels from small Burgundian coopers, only a small share of them new; in later vintages fermentation starts in tank before the wine is racked to barrel. It rests on its lees for about ten months, with little stirring, and the malolactic is allowed or held back as the year asks.
wine.glass: Wet stone and tart apple with lemon and pear, gaining hazelnut and honey with age; medium in body and dry, with a light touch of oak and long, bracing acidity.
wine.ageing: Tight when young, it opens after three to five years and keeps for a decade in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 11 to 13 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle briefly if it seems closed; a Burgundy glass.

label.means: The estate vineyard around the winery on top of the Blue Ridge, first planted in 1985.
The state of origin; the vineyard lies high on the Blue Ridge in Fauquier County.

records.table: Altitude high on the Blue Ridge in Fauquier County keeps Linden Vineyards' Hardscrabble Chardonnay taut: a white from the home vineyard, fermented in barrel and aged on its lees, to be poured a little cool in a Burgundy glass.
records.story: Linden began in 1983, when its founder and his family bought a long abandoned apple orchard on the Blue Ridge near the hamlet of Linden, after years of looking for high ground with east facing slopes. The first vines went in in 1985, Chardonnay among them, and that first block became the Hardscrabble vineyard around the winery, which was finished in time for the harvest of 1987, the first commercial vintage. Over the following decades the house became known for wines of single vineyards, adding Avenius, planted in 1996 half a mile to the north on a steep, east facing slope, and Boisseau, a warmer, west facing site at Front Royal about six miles away. The house's notes show its Chardonnay changing with it: fermented wholly in barrel in the late 1990s, with the malolactic partial in 1998, stopped in 1999 and full in 2000, and from 2012 started in tank and moved to barrel after a few weeks, with little new oak and less stirring, for freshness. Hardscrabble Red, a Bordeaux style blend, grows on the same slopes. Altitude and single vineyards are what Linden teaches in Virginia, and the Hardscrabble Chardonnay is the white that shows both.

wine.name: Lost Mountain
wine.grapes: A Bordeaux style blend: Cabernet Sauvignon leads in most vintages, with Merlot, Cabernet Franc and Petit Verdot in shares that change, and in some years Cabernet Franc leads.
wine.sites: The estate's own knoll at Delaplane in the Blue Ridge foothills, on steep slopes of thin, gravelly topsoil over deep decomposed granite that drains the summer rain away.
wine.making: Each year the blend is drawn afresh from the knoll's parcels, with a Bordeaux consultant who has worked beside the cellar since the first vintage, 2008. The wine is aged in French oak barrels before bottling at the estate.
wine.glass: Cassis, black cherry and blackberry over graphite, cedar and a savoury edge; full in body, with silky, fine grained tannin, fresh acidity and a long finish.
wine.ageing: Firm when young, it needs five to eight years, and a strong vintage keeps well beyond a decade.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two; a Bordeaux glass.

records.table: A granite knoll in the Blue Ridge foothills at Delaplane grows Lost Mountain, the grand red of RdV Vineyards: a Bordeaux style blend, Cabernet Sauvignon led in most years, made with a Bordeaux consultant since 2008, which wants decanting while young.
records.story: RdV takes its name from its founder's initials. A former Marine who had worked in technology, he went looking in the northern Virginia foothills for ground that would drain, and in 2004, by most accounts, settled on a rocky knoll at Delaplane, land once labelled not suitable for agriculture, where thin, gravelly topsoil lies over deep granite. From the first vintage, 2008, a Bordeaux consultant worked beside the cellar on two red blends only: Rendezvous, led by Merlot, and Lost Mountain, the grand wine, named for the place where it grows. In June 2024 the estate was sold to the family behind Château Montrose, the second growth of Saint-Estèphe, and the founder stepped back. The new owners announced that the estate would take the name of its grand wine and become Lost Mountain Vineyards. Lost Mountain belongs beside Bordeaux in a blind flight, and it comes from a house that under its founder made two wines and nothing else.

wine.name: Locksley Reserve Norton
wine.grapes: Norton, the great majority, blended in the 2021 and other later vintages with Tannat and a little Petit Verdot, in earlier ones with Nebbiolo; the blend changes yearly.
wine.sites: The Locksley Estate near Middleburg in Loudoun County, where Norton, first planted in 1998, leads the vineyard.
wine.making: Made from Norton grown on the house's own estate, its blend reworked each vintage. Norton's own deep colour and bright acidity carry the wine; Tannat adds tannin and Petit Verdot depth, in parts that have shifted over the years, with Nebbiolo in at least one vintage.
wine.glass: Dried cherry, wild berry and red plum with black pepper, smoke, vanilla and wet earth; deep purple in colour, bright and juicy in acidity rather than tannic, firm and velvety.
wine.ageing: Approachable on release, it keeps for a decade, its acidity holding it as the fruit dries.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant for an hour; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The native American grape raised in Richmond in the 1820s, once sold as Norton's Virginia Seedling.
Named for the Locksley Estate, the house's farm near Middleburg; the house's reserve red.

records.table: Norton, Virginia's own grape, raised in Richmond in the 1820s, fills Locksley Reserve, the reserve red of Chrysalis Vineyards near Middleburg: deep in colour and bright in acidity, with a little Tannat for grip. Its 2021 took gold at the Virginia Governor's Cup of 2024.
records.story: Norton is the grape a Richmond physician, Daniel Norborne Norton, who died in 1842, is believed to have raised in the 1820s; a Long Island nurseryman's catalogue listed it in 1822 as Norton's Virginia Seedling. It thrived where European vines failed, travelled west to Hermann, Missouri, in the 1840s, and in 1873 a Norton from Hermann took a gold medal at the Vienna World's Fair. Missouri kept the grape alive through Prohibition, and it came back to Virginia only in 1989. Chrysalis was founded to champion it: its founder planted the first Norton at the Locksley Estate near Middleburg in 1998, and by the house's account it was the largest planting of that first year. The house holds that it grows the largest single planting of Norton anywhere, a claim of its own, beside Albariño, Viognier and other European grapes. Locksley Reserve, its Norton led red, took a gold medal at the Virginia Governor's Cup of 2024 with its 2021 vintage, by the house's account the first gold for a Norton there. Locksley Reserve shows a guest what Virginia's own grape tastes like, and it sits well beside a Missouri Norton.

report: The label is confirmed as Locksley Reserve Norton by Virginia Wine's page for the wine and by the house; the house names Locksley Reserve its flagship, so the pick stands.

founded is left empty: Virginia Living has the land bought in 1997 and Norton planted in 1998, another account has the land bought in 1998, and Visit Loudoun has first vines in 1997; the story teaches only the Norton of 1998.
Daniel Norborne Norton's death in 1842 is in two sources, but his birth year is 1791 in one and 1794 in another, so no full dates are given.
The 2021's gold of 2024 rests on Middleburg Life and Northern Virginia Magazine; the first Norton gold is the house's own claim and is hedged.
The blend of 2021 (mostly Norton, with Tannat and Petit Verdot) is the house's; the 2009 carried Nebbiolo by the house's page; no source gave the barrel regimen.
The Agricultural and Forestal District of 2009 rests on one blog only and is cut; the founder is living and is not named.

changed: founded: was 1998; now empty, since the land is dated 1997 by Virginia Living and Visit Loudoun and 1998 by another account; the Norton planting of 1998 is kept.

story, table and card: was the first Norton to win Governor's Cup gold, told as fact; now the gold of 2024 for the 2021, by Middleburg Life and Northern Virginia Magazine, and the first for a Norton as the house's own claim.

story: the Agricultural and Forestal District of 2009 cut, in one source only; Norton's raising now told as believed, in the 1820s, the catalogue as a Long Island nurseryman's, and the move to Hermann in the 1840s added, by Missouri Wine.

wine.grapes and the question's explanation: was Tannat and Petit Verdot from 2017 to 2021; now the 2021 and later vintages, with Nebbiolo in earlier ones, as the house's pages for 2009 and 2021 give it.
wine.glass: was untested; now dried cherry, wild berry, red plum, black pepper, smoke, vanilla and wet earth, by the house's note and tastings of 2010.
sources: one source gives way to the Middleburg Life page that carries a fact now taught.
open: The largest single planting of Norton anywhere is the house's claim, told as such.
